Every distribution has an origin story. Ours has sorcerers, a vanishing act, a three-way split and a moon. Here it is, told the way the Moon keeps time: one phase at a time, from one new moon to the next.
Rewind to the turn of the millennium. No GitHub, no continuous integration, no containers. Most Linux users installed prebuilt packages and hoped the defaults suited them.

asked a cheeky question: what if your computer built everything itself? Sorcerer fetched software straight from the people who wrote it, compiled it on your own machine, let you choose the optional parts, and kept its package manager small enough to read in an afternoon.

As Sorcerer grew, so did the arguments about where it was heading and who got to decide. In late 2001 and early 2002, a small group of its developers forked it.
. It wasn't a rebellion for the fun of it: the idea was to keep Sorcerer's technology alive and keep improving it together, in the open. Lunar Penguin was soon renamed
, and the Lunar-Penguin name stayed on as an umbrella for any sister projects that might follow.

The moon and the penguin were already in the family: Chuck Mead's consulting firm was called MoonGroup, and its website ran a comic about a penguin called Dirty Bird. By March 2002 lunar-penguin.org greeted visitors with "Lunar Penguin is out of this world!", a tagline that would still be in the #lunar topic twenty years later. On 28 March 2002 Chuck cleared up the name: "Lunar-Penguin is actually a development group. Lunar-Linux is the group's first product."
The first piece of magic to get a new name was the spell-caster itself. On 19 May 2002 Kagan Kongar, Lunar's main developer at the time, rewrote Sorcerer's
, and kept the old copyright notices in its header "just in case some code is left :=)". Open
today and that note is still sitting at the top.
The oldest commit that survives in our repositories is dated
: Chuck Mead's "Initial revision" of the package manager, carried over from the project's original CVS repository. The moonbase's history starts on the very same day.
Six weeks later, on 1 October 2002, Lunar 1.0 lifted off. Its codename was

, after Chuck's comic penguin, and the announcement thanked the whole crew, with Kagan Kongar as lead developer. The very first comment underneath it read: "Lunar Linux is less a distribution than a programming project between friends." It was meant as a jab. We'll take it as a compliment.

Then came the eclipse. Not long after Lunar appeared, Sorcerer vanished from the internet. Its users suddenly couldn't update their systems, and developers scrambled to rebuild the distribution from backups and whatever copies they had lying around.

Kyle Sallee eventually returned and picked Sorcerer back up, but under a new license, the Sorcerer Public License, written to stop anyone from forking it again. Most of the remaining developers rebuilt the earlier GPL version from their backups instead. Out of respect for Kyle's wishes they gave up the Sorcerer name, voted on a new one, and became Source Mage, with a motto worthy of the family: "Linux so advanced, it may as well be magic."
When the dust settled, one distribution had become three:

Source Mage set out to build ever more powerful package management. Lunar went the other way, and has stuck with it ever since:
most of the system is shell scripts you can open and read.
things change carefully, never just for the sake of it.
stay close to upstream and patch only when you have to.
modules stay understandable and nothing hides the machinery.
While other distributions raced toward binary convenience or ever-thicker layers of automation, Lunar kept one promise:
The user should always be able to understand what the system is doing.
That made Lunar a home for administrators, developers and the plain curious: people who would rather know how their system works than have it work by magic.
Changes poured into the moonbase and ISOs rolled off the launch pad. Mission control was a single machine called

, which carried the CVS repository, the mail and the downloads all at once. When it went dark in November 2003, the #lunar topic sent everyone to mirrors in Denmark, the Netherlands and a university machine in Berlin. In August 2004 Lunar moved to a new server,
, and shared it with a neighbour: xfce.org. Together they went by foo-projects.org, short for "free Opensource Oriented projects".

There was a new face, too. In December 2003 Lunar got a new logo, which the channel promptly called "menacing and evil". It looked great on the login screen, and it stayed Lunar's face for nearly two decades, until a new logo arrived in 2022: the one at the top of this page.

After 1.7.0 the releases paused, and the public channels went quiet. From the outside it looked as if Lunar had drifted out of orbit.
Every year or two a stranger floated into #lunar to ask whether Lunar was still alive. In August 2016 the question was barely two minutes old when the build bot answered for us: "
moonbase-core build #737 – elfutils: version bumped to 0.167." Not the most flattering reply, but definitely a pulse.

That bot had joined the channel in November 2014, the voice of a new Jenkins server that tested every change. Like the servers it ran on, it was kept going year after year, quietly, the way good ground crews do. The bot built the moonbase's changes and reported every result in #lunar: nearly 3,900 of them by May 2021. In August 2017 the ISO started building itself every day, announced in the channel with quiet pride: "Three successful daily isos in a row!" The daily builds have been rolling off the pad ever since. In October 2017 we finally said it out loud:
we are still very much alive
And we were. The releases had paused, but the moonbase never did. Here is every year since that first commit, one moon each. The fuller the moon, the more changes landed in the moonbase that year:
Even the quietest full year, 2012, the year of the big split, saw more than 3,000 changes. Quiet skies, busy moonbase.
Since then the tools have changed, the way tools do.
In May 2021 freenode, home of #lunar since before our oldest logs, changed hands, and most of its staff walked out to start Libera.Chat. We

and left a note in the old channel's topic pointing the way. Five days later freenode's new owners took the channel over: the note itself was "in violation of freenode policy". Some of us still remembered 2006, when the #lunar topic read "RIP Rob, Thanks for everything" for Rob Levin, the founder of freenode.
Continuous integration still checks every contribution, and a linter now reads every module. Since March 2026 there's also moonbeam, the newest member of the crew: ask it on IRC for a version bump (
), and an AI agent does the work and opens the pull request, which CI then builds like any other. By November 2026 it had opened more than 1,100 of them. On this site, the
shows modules landing in the moonbase as it happens.
None of that changed what Lunar is.
Strip away the tools and Lunar is what it was on the first day:

Lunar's story isn't really about a Linux distribution. It's about a community that chose openness over control, kept the ideas worth keeping, and preferred understanding technology to just consuming it. Around 200 people have left their mark in our repositories so far, and they've shown that a small crew held together by shared values and plain curiosity can stay in orbit far longer than anyone expected.
Every lunar month ends the way it began, with a new moon, and the next cycle is already rising: Lunar 1.8.0 is built every day.

The Moon keeps going. So does Lunar.
